chunks: For you have made your religion subservient to the worldly seekings of a man whose misguidance is evident and whose veil has been torn away,
He mars an honourable man with his company and befools those who keep his society.
You are following in his footsteps and seeking his favours like the dog that follows the lion, clinging to its paws and waiting for whatever remnants of its prey fall down to it.
In this way, you have ruined your world as well as the next life!
Although if you had stuck to the right, you would have got what you were after.
If Allāh grants me power over you and Ibn Abī Sufyān (Mu‘āwiyah), I shall award you both recompense of what you have done,
but if you escape and survive then hereafter there is only evil for you both; and that is an end to the matter.

key_terms.الضِّرْغَامُ: The lion (metaphor for the powerful leader)

ai.seo_question: What is the metaphor used in Nahj al-Balagha to describe Amr ibn al-As's subservience to worldly power?
ai.summary: In this letter to Amr ibn al-As, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) critiques the Umayyad strategy of subordinating religious authority to worldly power, using the vivid metaphor of a dog clinging to a lion's claws to illustrate blind subservience. This passage highlights the Shia scholarly view that political pragmatism often leads to the erosion of spiritual integrity, warning that such compromise ultimately ruins both one's dunya and akhirah. The promise of recompense underscores the divine justice that will befall those who prioritize temporal gain over truth.
